item.title: Low-Overhead Quantum Error Correction with Boundary-Connected Planar Modules
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Constructing modular hyperbolic surface and color codes by wiring static boundary connections between Euclidean planar modules reduces physical qubit overhead by ≥10× compared to planar surface codes under circuit-level noise. Larger modular codes reach encoding rate k/n=1/16 with distance d≥22, exceeding the [[288,12,18]] bivariate bicycle code.

Grade 0.536 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Oscar Higgott, Hasan Sayginel, Francisco J. H. Heras, Zhiyang He, Tomas Jochym-O'Connor, Andrew W. Senior, Lei M. Zhang, Thomas Edlich, James S. Spencer, Matt McEwen, Craig Gidney, Johannes Bausch, Pushmeet Kohli, Hartmut Neven

Asks

Can low-overhead quantum error-correcting codes be implemented using mostly nearest-neighbor connectivity on flat planar modules connected only via sparse boundary links?

Before

Planar surface codes require high physical qubit overhead; standard high-rate LDPC codes like the [[288,12,18]] bivariate bicycle code require non-planar 2D routing across all qubits.

But

Circuit-level numerical simulations, assumes static inter-module links restricted to module boundaries and standard depolarizing noise models.

Tools

Semi-hyperbolic surface and color codes · Boundary-connected Euclidean planar modules · Circuit-level noise simulations · Neural network and minimum-weight perfect matching decoders · Fault-tolerant walking circuits

Abstract

Realizing practical quantum computers requires quantum error correction, but the most widely implemented approach, the planar surface code, demands a substantial physical qubit overhead. Here, we demonstrate that partitioning quantum processors into manageable, flat modules with non-local inter-module connections provides a natural solution. By wiring sparse, static boundary connections between Euclidean planar modules, we construct modular hyperbolic surface and color codes, based on new families of semi-hyperbolic codes. Using modular syndrome extraction circuits and efficient neural network and matching decoders, our circuit-level simulations show that this modular memory design can reduce the physical qubit overhead by tenfold or more compared to the surface code, even under elevated inter-module seam error rates. Projecting to larger system sizes, we find modular codes with encoding rate k/n=1/16 and distance d≥22, exceeding both the rate and distance of the [[288,12,18]] two-gross bivariate bicycle code while using mostly nearest-neighbor gates within planar modules, and implying an over 30× overhead reduction relative to surface codes. We develop fault-tolerant walking circuits for implementing logic via code automorphisms, which we co-design with low-weight, highly symmetrical logical bases and a modular extractor system that is ≈4.5× smaller than the code itself. Combining these methods, our modular memory can be used as dense storage in a universal fault-tolerant architecture, unlocking the efficiency of high-rate codes without sacrificing the fabrication advantages of planar modules.

item.title: SpiderCSS: Scalable Fault-Tolerant CSS State Preparation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Constructs fault-tolerant CSS state preparation circuits via polynomial-time ZX-calculus rewrites, lowering logical error rate by an average of 33.7%, raising acceptance rate by 9.5%, and cutting CNOT count by up to 53.8% across codes up to distance 15.

Grade 0.526 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Boldizsár Poór, Andrey Boris Khesin, Sarah Meng Li, Benjamin Rodatz, John van de Wetering, Richie Yeung

Figure

Scatter plots of percentage improvements of SpiderCSS over the FaO baseline for CSS states up to distance 15. The left panel shows logical error rate reduction vs. acceptance rate increase; the right panel shows circuit depth reduction vs. active qubit count reduction under footprint- and depth-optimizing reuse.

Asks

How can fault-tolerant CSS state preparation circuits be synthesized scalably with reduced circuit depth and qubit overhead?

Before

Flag at Origin (FaO) modular flagged gadgets (Khesin et al. 2024), limited by offline gadget generation and large depth.

But

Restricted to CSS states and CSS noise (standard unidealization rules fail for non-CSS stabilizer codes); evaluated under circuit-level depolarizing noise (p=10−3 and p=10−4); post-selection discards states with ≥d/2 syndrome faults.

Tools

ZX-calculus · Fault Tolerance by Construction framework · SpiderCat FT CAT-state synthesis · Stim Monte Carlo simulations · CP-SAT exact scheduler

Abstract

Fault-tolerant preparation of logical states is a critical primitive for the realization of large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing. This paper introduces SpiderCSS, a scalable compilation pipeline that generates highly-optimized, fault-tolerant state preparation circuits for arbitrary Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes. Starting from an idealized specification of a CSS state, we use the ZX-calculus and fault-equivalent rewrites to construct a diagram that prepares the given state while preserving the fault tolerance of the initial ideal ZX-diagram. From this diagram, SpiderCSS constructs a fault-tolerant CSS-state preparation circuit using a modular construction that is CNOT-minimal both within each component and also in the way these components are connected together. By only using fault-equivalent rewrites, the final circuit is provably fault-tolerant without needing expensive verification. Monte Carlo simulations across a variety of CSS codes up to distance 15 show that SpiderCSS scales efficiently and constructs circuits with substantially reduced depth and qubit footprint compared to existing scalable and heuristic methods, while simultaneously achieving an average decrease of 33.7% in logical error rate and an increase of 9.5% in acceptance rate.

item.title: Fault-tolerant and fully addressable unitary logical gates via round-robin sparsification
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Round-robin circuits sparsified via stabilizer deformations implement fully addressable, fault-tolerant transversal CZ gates with circuit depth independent of code distance for 2D translationally invariant qLDPC codes. On a 288-qubit gross code (d=12), the addressable tCZ achieves ∼4× lower spacetime overhead and ∼5× lower logical error impact than code surgery.

Grade 0.505 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Kaavya Sahay, Cody Jones

Figure

Logical error rate versus physical error rate for the 288-qubit d=12 gross code comparing an addressable transversal CZ against code surgery (XX measurement) and quantum memory baselines, showing fault-tolerant error suppression.

Asks

How can fully addressable, fault-tolerant, low-depth transversal logical two-qubit Clifford gates be realized on quantum low-density parity check codes without multi-round code surgery?

Before

Addressable logical operations on qLDPC codes relied primarily on lattice surgery taking O(d) measurement rounds, or on transversal constructions limited in code distance or stabilizer structure.

But

Restricted to 2D translationally invariant qLDPC codes, evaluated primarily on periodic boundary conditions; complex codes with incomplete disjoint representative sets require either an intermediate stabilizer round to restore full distance d or accept distance reduction to d/2.

Tools

Round-robin sparsification · Stabilizer deformations · Cylinder trick (sliding cylinder) · Stim/Stimflow numerical simulations

Abstract

For quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) codes, the ability to manipulate individual logical units of information, i.e. the use of addressable gates, enables maximal utility of their efficient encoding. We introduce explicit low-depth unitary circuits that realize fully addressable and fault-tolerant two-qubit Clifford gates for a subset of two-dimensional translationally invariant qLDPC codes. Our transversal unitaries are created by applying a geometrically structured sparsification procedure to round-robin circuits. We verify the general applicability of our protocol by proposing and numerically simulating a range of addressable CZs between toric, cyclic hypergraph-product, color, gross, and directional codes, demonstrating fault-tolerant memory-like logical error rate scaling.

item.title: Single-Shot Error Correction at Optimal Spacetime Cost
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Encoded quantum memory achieves optimal spacetime cost C=O(S(K+log⁡(S/ε))) using an explicit noisy syndrome extraction circuit and O(N) classical decoding work per cycle. Relative spacetime overhead C/(KS)=O(1+log⁡(S/ε)/K) is constant for K=Ω(log⁡(S/ε)).

Grade 0.500 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Kishor Bharti, Tobias Haug, Derek Khu, Andrew Tanggara

Figure

Schematic of optimal memory protocol: single-round check measurements and fixed-iteration decoding maintain residual error below the correctable threshold, sharing the O(log⁡(S/ε)) reliability overhead across K logical qubits over S cycles.

Asks

Can the optimal spacetime cost Ω(S(K+log⁡(S/ε))) for storing K logical qubits for S steps with error at most ε be attained using realistic, noisy quantum error correction circuits and efficient decoding?

Before

Lower bound Ω(S(K+log⁡(S/ε))) was matched only under idealized error correction (Bharti et al. 2024); independent surface code patches require O(KSlog2⁡(KS/ε)).

But

Requires long-range qubit connectivity, fast and reliable parallel classical processing, error strength below threshold p<p∗, and input/output remaining encoded in the code blocks.

Tools

quantum Tanner codes · single-shot decoding · local-stochastic circuit noise model · Knill-Laflamme conditions for coherent errors

Abstract

Recent work established that, for independent erasures, storing K logical qubits for S time steps with error at most ε requires a spacetime cost of Ω(S(K+log(S/ε))). A matching construction was also given, but assumes ideal error correction. Here we show that the same scaling can be achieved with an explicit noisy error-correction circuit and efficient decoding, counting all state-preparation, gate, measurement, and wait locations, provided that the hardware supports long-range qubit connectivity and fast, reliable classical processing. Thus, reliability adds only a logarithmic overhead shared by all stored qubits. The construction works for sufficiently weak but otherwise general circuit noise, including faults during syndrome extraction and correlated faults, and for independent erasures it matches the best known lower bound up to constant factors. We attain this scaling using quantum Tanner codes, with each memory step consisting of one round of syndrome extraction followed by a fixed number of parallel classical decoder steps that reduce the residual error enough to keep later faults correctable, regardless of memory size, storage time, or target accuracy. Together, this gives exponentially small failure probability per step while keeping the cost of each memory step linear in the code size. The same analysis also extends to certain constant-depth logical Clifford operations.

item.title: Fault tolerance of quantum circuits with tensor networks and symplectic geometry
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Establishes operator-algebraic necessary and sufficient conditions for quantum circuit fault tolerance under general noise, yielding closed-form detection and logical-effect matrices for stabilizer circuits and linear-programming upper bounds on circuit distance.

Grade 0.485 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Soham Ghosh, Holger Boche, Andrew Tanggara

Figure

A two-round adaptive quantum circuit interacting with causally correlated noise via instrument modules, classical measurement records, and noise memory systems before a final noiseless recovery operation.

Asks

How can fault tolerance and circuit distance be certified and bounded algebraically across general and stabilizer quantum circuits under arbitrary noise models?

But

Non-adaptive stabilizer circuits for closed-form matrices; independent and identically distributed depolarizing noise for weight-enumerator pseudothreshold bounds.

Tools

Quantum-comb formalism · Semidefinite programming (SDP) · Linear programming (LP) · Symplectic geometry · MacWilliams identities

Abstract

We develop an operator-algebraic framework for analyzing fault tolerance in quantum circuits and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for fault tolerance under any given noise model. For prescribed circuit families and noise models, we derive a semidefinite program (SDP) based test whose infeasibility certifies that there does not exist any recovery map restoring its intended operation. For non-adaptive stabilizer circuits, analyzing the stabilizer symmetries of its components with symplectic geometry, we obtain closed-form detection and logical-effect matrices that characterize circuit distance algebraically. Applied to a finite Hastings--Haah honeycomb Floquet-code circuit, these matrices certify the dynamical encoding of two logical qubits and distance four under Pauli noise including measurement errors. Using these matrices, we then derive MacWilliams identities for circuit weight enumerators and obtain linear-programming (LP) upper bounds on circuit distance. Output-code constraints give additional Singleton-like bounds. Under independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) depolarizing noise, the weight enumerators determine decoder failure probabilities and yield upper bounds on finite-circuit pseudothresholds. Finally, we derive LP distance bounds for families of flag syndrome-extraction circuits specified by their CNOT orderings, by incorporating the t-flag criterion as additional linear constraints to the distance-bounding LP. An analytical CSS Hamming-code benchmark yields a tight distance-three bound attained by the Chao--Reichardt one-flag construction.

item.title: High-Rate Quantum Codes with Proven Distance and Low-Weight Measurements
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Proves dressed distance is D=2L for any L-dimensional rectangular subsystem code with even side lengths qi≥4, data qubits N=∏iqi, and logical qubits K=∏i(qi−2), with max gauge measurement weight w=maxi⁡qi.

Grade 0.482 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Kishor Bharti, Tobias Haug, Runzhou Tao, Kevin Ye

Figure

Protected encoding rate K/N plotted against maximum gauge measurement weight w for code distances D=16,32,64 under a cap of at most 10,000 data qubits.

Asks

How many logical qubits can a finite quantum memory protect under low-weight gauge measurements on rectangular coordinate grids?

Before

Uniform side-four and side-six subsystem many-hypercube codes (Nakai and Goto), plus standard subsystem products like SHYPS(6) which achieves [[3969,36,3249,32]] with rate 0.91% vs 13.17% (65 line-gauge code) at distance 32.

But

Static code distance; does not evaluate fault-tolerant circuit distance, noise thresholds, decoder performance, or geometric locality constraints.

Tools

subsystem codes · binary symplectic formalism · quotient-space distance proof · Lean 4 interactive theorem prover

Code. https://github.com/VerifiedQC/Lean-QEC/tree/subsystem-codes/LeanQEC/Stabilizer/Subsystem

Abstract

We study a family of quantum subsystem codes defined on rectangular coordinate grids of any dimension, with even side lengths of at least four. The directly measured operators act along coordinate lines. For every member of the family, we derive the number of protected logical qubits and prove its dressed distance without a numerical search. To illustrate the resulting design choices, we impose a budget of at most 10,000 data qubits and determine the complete tradeoff between encoding rate and measurement weight within this family at distances 16, 32, and 64. At distance 16, one code protects 4,096 logical qubits among 10,000 data qubits using weight-ten measurements. At distances 32 and 64, codes with 7,776 and 9,216 data qubits protect 1,024 and 256 logical qubits, respectively, using weight-six measurements. We include and explain Lean code snippets throughout the paper to guide readers through the formal verification of our subsystem-code construction and its dressed and bare distances.

item.arxave:abstract: We study a family of quantum subsystem codes defined on rectangular coordinate grids of any dimension, with even side lengths of at least four. The directly measured operators act along coordinate lines. For every member of the family, we derive the number of protected logical qubits and prove its dressed distance without a numerical search. To illustrate the resulting design choices, we impose a budget of at most 10,000 data qubits and determine the complete tradeoff between encoding rate and measurement weight within this family at distances 16, 32, and 64. At distance 16, one code protects 4,096 logical qubits among 10,000 data qubits using weight-ten measurements. At distances 32 and 64, codes with 7,776 and 9,216 data qubits protect 1,024 and 256 logical qubits, respectively, using weight-six measurements. We include and explain Lean code snippets throughout the paper to guide readers through the formal verification of our subsystem-code construction and its dressed and bare distances.

item.title: Efficient fidelity simulation of high-rate magic distillation circuits
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Monte Carlo sampling of syndrome statistics, logical fidelity, and Pauli expectation values for noisy circuits with X, CNOT, and level-3 Clifford-hierarchy diagonal gates runs in 𝒪(n3T) time per sample, with zero scaling dependence on the number of logical qubits.

Grade 0.480 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Xiao Xiao, Dominik Hangleiter, J. Pablo Bonilla Ataides, Rohan Mehta, Varun Menon, Mikhail D. Lukin, Michael J. Gullans

Figure

Plots total physical ancilla overhead against logical infidelity of a 9-qubit hypergraph state prepared via a depth-2 CCZ circuit on three [[27,3,3]] tricycle code blocks across syndrome extraction protocols.

Asks

How can one efficiently benchmark the fault-tolerant logical performance and syndrome distributions of quantum circuits containing non-Clifford gates under stochastic Pauli noise?

Before

Generic exact classical benchmarking incurred a cost exponential in the number of non-Clifford gates or magic measures, or depended separately on the number of logical qubits.

But

Circuit components restricted to X, CNOT, and level-3 diagonal gates (plus Clifford pre/post-processing); syndrome checks must be affected by faults from a constant number of layers; restricted to circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise.

Tools

Affine-diagonal normal form · Clifford-hierarchy commutator reduction · Monte Carlo fault-path backpropagation · Binary Gaussian elimination syndrome sampling

Abstract

Non-Clifford gates are essential for avoiding classical simulability under the Gottesman-Knill theorem. An error-corrected circuit with non-Clifford gates will therefore be an important element for realizing useful fault-tolerant quantum algorithms. However, accurately understanding the fault-tolerant performance of such circuits faces challenges due to the classical hardness of simulating these circuits. We avoid simulating logical measurements and develop exact and efficient classical methods for benchmarking circuits composed of X, CNOT, and diagonal gates in the Clifford hierarchy, including state and gate teleportation gadgets with feedforward. For circuits with third-level diagonal gates, our benchmarking algorithm efficiently samples syndrome statistics and estimates the output logical fidelity and expectation values of certain Clifford observables, including all Pauli observables. The evaluation of syndrome expectation values also extends to circuits with fourth-level diagonal gates. Our algorithm scales polynomially in the number of physical qubits n and circuit depth T, independent of the number of logical qubits. The benchmarking applications include IQP sampling and magic state preparation/cultivation. We demonstrate the practical utility of our simulation algorithms by using them to optimize high-rate magic state distillation factories based on three copies of a [[27,3,3]] tricycle code.

item.title: Exact Recovery for Non-Abelian Surface Codes
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Constructs an exact, deterministic quantum recovery unitary that moves errors onto ancillas to be projected out for topological surface codes based on the quantum double D(G) of any finite group G.

Grade 0.465 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Alison Warman, Nathanan Tantivasadakarn, Sakura Schafer-Nameki

Figure

Charge transfer circuits that map the irreducible representation error on a direct-lattice edge entering or exiting vertex v onto an ancilla qudit via controlled operations.

Asks

How can exact, deterministic error recovery be realized on 2D non-Abelian quantum double surface codes D(G) given non-invertible anyon fusion and non-Abelian stabilizers?

Before

Thresholds and existence proofs were known, along with explicit recovery for Abelian G, repeated-round anyon decoders, or restricted setups like D(D4) via just-in-time decoding; general explicit recovery unitaries were missing.

But

Requires predetermined neutral correctable error clusters and perfect syndrome measurements as input; decoder/syndrome extraction circuit construction is left to future work.

Tools

Kitaev quantum double D(G) · group algebra irreducible representation error basis · stabilizer gauge-fixing · flux and charge transfer circuits · ancilla projection

Abstract

We study exact recovery for non-Abelian topological surface codes based on the quantum double D(G) of any finite group G. We determine an orthogonal error basis, that is comprised of group multiplication and irreducible representation operators. Whenever the errors are supported on closed loops on the lattice or dual lattice, there is a redundancy in the basis, due to stabilizers. To remedy this, we introduce a gauge-fixing that results in a complete and orthogonal error basis on the code space. Assuming as input predetermined, neutral correctable error clusters, we construct charge and flux transfer circuits that move the errors onto ancillas that then get projected out. This is an exact and deterministic recovery protocol, applicable to surface codes for any finite, in particular non-Abelian, group G.
